text.content:
Since the diablerie of their Antediluvian Saulot at the hands of the Tremere, the surviving Salubri have split into three uneasy castes, sometimes called the Triumvirate. Each traces its lineage to a different response to Saulot's teachings and to the clan's near-annihilation, and the three rarely trust one another fully.

  • The Healers follow the original vocation Saulot taught: mending broken bodies and souls, seeking Golconda, and refusing to harm even in self-defense. They are the best known (and most persecuted) face of the clan, and the fewest in number.
  • The Warriors descend from Samiel, Saulot's rebellious childe, who left the healer's path to train among the Brujah and Gangrel before dying leading the Cainite host against the Baali in the vale of Gehenna. Warriors follow the Code of Samiel, hunt the infernal without mercy, and increasingly turn their swords on the Tremere.
  • The Watchers are a barely-attested third caste, spoken of only in whispers even by other Salubri. Healers and warriors alike are reluctant to discuss them, and some deny they exist at all; what little is known suggests they keep their own counsel, maintain a fixation on events at Ceoris (the Tremere's chantry-city), and address warriors as "brothers" while speaking of healers only dismissively.

All three castes bear a third eye once they progress beyond the most basic uses of Valeren; its origin is debated even among the Salubri themselves, though most agree it is somehow bound up with the Discipline rather than an inherent trait of the bloodline.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two: The Triumvirate.

pages.name: The Code of Samiel and the Blooding

text.content:
The warrior caste traces its founding rite to the Code of Samiel, a lost text said to have been dictated in part by Samiel himself and completed by his successor Uriel and his coterie after Samiel's death at the Baali's hands in the vale of Gehenna. The Code governs a warrior's conduct in war and peace, and — most crucially — sets down the rite of the Blooding, a second and deeply private rite of passage undergone after the Embrace and years of training.

Where the Embrace grants unlife, the Blooding is described by those who have undergone it as an acceptance of spiritual sacrifice: the childe is tested on knowledge and composure (traditionally through ritual lashes meant to provoke and test control of the Beast), made to recite the Code from memory, and given a new name — the name by which Samiel is said to summon his warriors forth at Judgment. Most warrior lines today trace their lineage to one of five grandsires who survived Samiel's fall: Uriel, Za'aphiel, Ezrael, Aariel, and Gabriel. True copies of the Code are believed largely lost since the Tremere purges began, and warriors blooded by lesser, reconstructed rites are said by some elders to be subtly "lesser" for it.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two: The Triumvirate.

pages.name: The Baali Wars and the Gnostic Purges

text.content:
Long before the Tremere's usurpation, the Salubri fought a war that shaped the clan's warrior caste. When rumors of an infernalist cult — the Baali — spread from the river valleys near the Second City, Saulot sent four warriors to investigate; only one returned, driven near-mad, to report that two had been diablerized and that the mission had been betrayed from within by one of their own. Enraged, Saulot demanded war, and Samiel led an assembled host of every clan into the vale of Gehenna. The Baali were driven back but Samiel was slain by treachery from behind, and over half his warriors and healers fell with him. The traitor was never conclusively identified or found.

Years later, acting on rumors that the traitor sheltered among Gnostic Cainite sects who had arrogated the mantle of the Church to feed on the faithful, Saulot personally hunted the Gnostics in what chroniclers call the Gnostic Purges. He never found the traitor, but the purges devastated the Gnostic sects and left a legacy of suspicion that still colors Salubri dealings with heretical or infernal-tainted Cainite religious movements.

These two wars are the wellspring of the warrior caste's abiding, near-obsessive crusade against the infernal (and, since the diablerie of Saulot, against the Tremere as well).

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Three: Miscellanea et Demonica.

A Hibernian warrior of Samiel's line (childe of Baradiel), Embraced around 700 AD and named for a legendary woman warrior and an early saint of her homeland. Tall, disciplined, and openly dismissive of using Valeren against foes she deems unworthy of it, she has bested Ventrue duelists barehanded and passed for a mere student in the training halls of an elder Brujah while concealing her third eye. Unusual among warriors for being one of the clan's few known female fighters, she has spoken candidly (if guardedly) about the difficulties women of the caste face gaining acceptance from other clans' training halls. A valuable primary source for chroniclers of the warrior caste, and a firm believer that Golconda remains open even to those who live by the sword.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two: The Triumvirate.

pages.name: Genevieve du Fortin, Healer of the Winter's Tale

text.content:
A young healer of noble birth who took holy orders to escape an unwanted marriage, Genevieve received a vision of an elder Salubri calling her to unlife while still a novice. She has mastered much of the healer's art and is recognized as a skilled midwife despite her relative youth (roughly a decade in the blood at the time she is best attested), and travels with a solicitous Scottish Gangrel companion named Chance. Her tale is emblematic of the healer caste's precarious existence: hosted by a mortal lord who came to suspect her of infernalism after Tremere accusations, she fled into the night rather than see her host's household torn apart on her account, taking his young son Hugh under her protection until he could safely be returned. She embodies the healer's dilemma — genuine compassion for mortals and Kindred alike, constantly weighed against the mortal danger that same compassion invites.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapters One and Two.

Said to have been one of Saulot's favored childer and a sister in blood to Samiel, Rayzeel was trained as a healer but is remembered less for her hands than for her music: a former slave of Enoch skilled with lyre and voice, her songs were among the few things able to soothe Saulot during his grief over Samiel's death and his own increasingly disturbing trances. Persistent rumor holds that her closeness to her sire went beyond that of childe and father, though no Salubri chronicler has found (or admitted to finding) conclusive proof. Rayzeel withdrew from the world around the time of Saulot's final torpor and her fate since is unknown; some believe she perished alongside Saulot's Amaranth, while others point to songs still circulating among the clan that bear what they believe is her unmistakable hand.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two: The Triumvirate.

pages.name: Yael and Matthias, Hunters of the Infernal

text.content:
Yael (born Althea of Phillipus), a warrior descended through Gabriel and Ithuriel from Samiel himself, is among the eldest attested warriors still active, possibly Embraced in the time of the ancient Greeks among horse-herding peoples of the north. A skilled archer said to have mastered both paths of Valeren, she has made crusading against the Baali and their infernal masters her unlife's sole purpose, drawing the wrath of infernalists wherever she travels.

Matthias of Bath, a healer of English holy orders, met Yael when she sought healing after battling a powerful Baali. The two forged a lasting partnership: Matthias rarely travels openly with Yael, instead working from within the Church to unearth her prey and secure resources on her behalf. Their joint treatises on the infernal are considered the standard scholarly work on the subject among the Salubri. Matthias was believed by some to be well along the path toward Golconda; later report holds that Tremere agents captured and slew him in an attempt to lure Yael into a trap, and that his third eye opened in his final agony, though what he saw in that moment is known only to Yael.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two: The Triumvirate.

The existence of a third Salubri caste, the Watchers, rests almost entirely on the testimony of a single self-described member, "Pazia," and a single intercepted letter. Embraced during the reign of the Byzantine empress Theodosia by a Salubri named Wenceslaus, Pazia served the imperial court as a healer before Saulot's diablerie (which she and others of her caste refer to obliquely as "the Great Event" or "the Wicked Day," never directly). She speaks of the healers dismissively as passive lambs to the slaughter, and of the warriors — whom she calls "brothers" with an ardor other Salubri find unsettling — as blades she and her caste mean to guide toward proper vengeance.

A subsequent letter attributed to Pazia's circle spoke of "watching the door of Ceoris" (the Tremere's chantry-fortress) and learning "a strange and mighty secret" regarding Saulot's diablerie, urging the warriors to stand ready for a day when "Ceoris' gates fly open and all things stand revealed." No healer or warrior interviewed on the subject will speak of the Watchers without unease, and several react with open superstition (spitting, warding gestures) at the mere mention. Whether the Watchers are a genuine, organized third caste, a handful of unaffiliated obsessives, or something else that quietly monitors the Tremere from the shadows remains one of the clan's most sensitive open questions.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two: The Triumvirate — "The Boke of the Watcher."

Nearly every Salubri who advances beyond the most basic uses of Valeren eventually manifests a third eye, usually hidden beneath the hair or a headcovering, that opens and sheds colored light (varying by power and temperament — a warrior's eye is often reported as glowing wrathful red, a healer's as soft gold) when certain Valeren powers are used. Scholarly consensus among the clan's chroniclers links the eye specifically to Valeren rather than to the bloodline itself, since Salubri healing gifts predate Saulot's eastern pilgrimage while the eye appeared only afterward, and the warriors' powers were devised independently by Samiel's line without any comparable mark. Rumors persist of long-lost, more prodigious uses of the eye — sight into the spirit world, or the naked souls of men and Cainites alike — but if such powers ever existed, none now walking are believed to know them. Watchers are noted to rarely display the eye at all, a fact some cite as evidence they make little practical use of Valeren despite understanding it.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Three: Miscellanea et Demonica.

pages.name: Salubri Customs: The Kiss, Feeding, and the Fallen Angels

text.content:
The Kiss: Saulot forbade the Embrace of children and forbade Embracing out of love or for companionship, punishing (even to final death, by some accounts) childer who transgressed — though persistent rumor holds that Saulot's own closeness to his childe Rayzeel may have skirted his own law.

Feeding: Saulot forbade his childer from feeding on any who feared them, a commandment healers hold to strictly, fostering their well-known good relations with mortal neighbors as a matter of survival. Warriors interpret the rule more loosely, reasoning that hatred and battle-rage are not fear, and feel free to feed on defeated foes.

Fallen Angels: In the chaos following Saulot's diablerie, a small number of warriors — two grandchilder of Aariel who renounced their birth names for the names of fallen angels — broke from the clan's councils, vowing to strike back at the Tremere regardless of the cost to their own souls. Their fate and whether they have turned to infernalism outright is unknown; the clan's remaining warriors regard the question of whether they must someday be hunted down as kin-slayers, or spared as fellow victims of the Tremere's crime, as one of the gravest unresolved questions facing the caste.

Source: Clanbook: Salubri, Chapter Two and Chapter Three.
